ai.literal: He hoarded abundant great wealth; he who does not enjoy that is a dead man; there is nothing remaining for him to do.
ai.translation: He who hoards vast, abundant wealth but does not enjoy it is as good as dead; there is nothing else left for him to do.
ai.modern: எல்லையைக் கடந்த பெரும் செல்வத்தைச் சேர்த்து வைத்து, அதனை அனுபவிக்காமல் வாழ்கின்றவன் இறந்தவனுக்கு ஒப்பாவான்; அவனால் செய்யக்கூடிய பயன் வேறு ஒன்றும் இல்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the absolute uselessness of hoarded wealth that is never put to use. The phrase 'வாய் சான்ற பெரும்பொருள்' describes a massive fortune that exceeds all normal limits. The poet argues that a person who hoards such wealth but does not consume or enjoy it ('அஃதுண்ணான்') is functionally equivalent to a dead person ('செத்தான்'). Just as a corpse cannot utilize worldly goods, the miser derives no benefit from his riches, leaving him with no active purpose or utility ('செயக்கிடந்தது இல்') in life.

ai.literal: By wealth is possible everything, thinking thus, without giving, he who hoards, by that delusion, arises an ignoble birth.
ai.translation: For the miser who hoards without giving, thinking that everything can be achieved through wealth, an ignoble birth will arise from that very delusion.
ai.modern: செல்வத்தினால் எல்லாம் முடியும் என்று எண்ணி, பிறருக்குக் கொடுக்காமல் சேர்த்து வைக்கும் பேராசைக்காரனுக்கு, அந்த அறியாமையினால் பெருமையற்ற பிறவி உண்டாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns against the delusion of hoarding wealth without sharing it. The miser falsely believes that money alone can secure everything in life, leading them to withhold charity. This mental blindness or delusion (maruḷ) is what ultimately causes them to be reborn into an ignoble, unworthy state (māṇāp piṟappu). The poet highlights that wealth is useless if not given to those in need, and the obsession with hoarding only degrades one's character and future.

ai.literal: Accumulation hoarding, fame not-desiring men's existence, to the earth a burden.
ai.translation: The very existence of men who hoard accumulated wealth greedily and do not desire good fame is a mere burden to the earth.
ai.modern: செல்வத்தைச் சேர்ப்பதிலேயே குறியாய் இருந்து, புகழை விரும்பாத மனிதர்களின் பிறப்பு, இந்த பூமிக்கு ஒரு பாரமே ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the futility of hoarding wealth without using it for noble deeds. The word 'ஈட்டம்' refers to the accumulation of riches, while 'இவறி' describes the act of hoarding it greedily. Those who hoard in this manner do not seek 'இசை' (fame), which is earned by being generous to others. The poet concludes that the 'தோற்றம்' (existence or birth) of such useless individuals is nothing but a 'பொறை' (heavy burden) to the 'நிலம்' (earth).

ai.literal: As a legacy, what indeed will he think [he leaves behind], he who is not loved by anyone?
ai.translation: What can a person who is loved by no one possibly think he is leaving behind as his legacy?
ai.modern: ஒருவராலும் விரும்பப்படாத ஒருவன், தனக்குப் பின் எஞ்சி நிற்கும் எச்சமாக எதை நினைப்பான்?
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the utter emptiness of a life lived without generosity. A wealthy person who does not share their wealth is not loved or desired ('nacca paṭāatavaṉ') by anyone in society. When such a person contemplates their legacy ('eccam'), which refers to what remains after death like children or a good reputation, they have nothing to look back on. Since they lived only for themselves, they leave behind no love, gratitude, or meaningful memory.

ai.literal: Giving and enjoying to those who do not have, piled-up crores though there are, nothing.
ai.translation: To those who neither give to others nor enjoy their wealth themselves, even if they possess piled-up crores of riches, they actually have nothing.
ai.modern: பிறருக்குக் கொடுப்பதும் தாம் அனுபவிப்பதும் இல்லாதவர்க்கு, அடுக்கடுக்கான கோடிப் பொருள்கள் இருந்தாலும் அதனால் ஒரு பயனும் இல்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the futility of hoarded wealth that is neither shared nor enjoyed. The poet uses the words 'கொடுப்பதூஉம்' (giving) and 'துய்ப்பதூஉம்' (enjoying) with poetic elongation to emphasize these two essential purposes of wealth. For those who lack both these actions, having even piled-up crores ('அடுக்கிய கோடி') of riches is equivalent to having nothing ('இல்'). True wealth is defined by its utility and generosity, not by its mere accumulation.

ai.literal: Ruin is the great wealth of him who does not enjoy it himself, and who does not have the nature of giving even a single thing to the deserving.
ai.translation: The immense wealth of a person who neither enjoys it himself nor has the nature of giving anything to those who deserve it is only a source of ruin.
ai.modern: தான் அனுபவிக்காமலும், தகுதியுடையவர்களுக்கு ஒன்றையும் கொடுக்காத இயல்பு உடையவனுடைய பெரிய செல்வம் அவனுக்குக் குற்றத்தையே அல்லது அழிவையே தரும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the useless and harmful nature of hoarded wealth. A person who possesses great wealth but does not use it for his own enjoyment, nor possesses the character to give even a small portion of it to deserving people, gains nothing from it. Instead, such unused and unshared wealth becomes a source of affliction or ruin ('ஏதம்') for him. The key words 'துவ்வான்' (one who does not enjoy) and 'ஈதல் இயல்பிலாதான்' (one who lacks the nature of giving) highlight the double failure of the miserly rich.

ai.literal: To the destitute even one thing he who does not give, his wealth, great beauty she who possessed, alone, having grown old, is like.
ai.translation: The wealth of one who gives nothing to the destitute is like a woman of great beauty growing old in lonely solitude.
ai.modern: வறியவர்களுக்கு ஏதும் தராதவனுடைய செல்வம், மிகுந்த அழகைப் பெற்ற ஒரு பெண் தனியாகவே இருந்து முதுமையடைவதைப் போன்றது.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses a vivid analogy to illustrate the uselessness of hoarded wealth. The word 'அற்றார்' refers to those who are completely destitute, and 'ஆற்றாதான்' is one who fails to perform the duty of giving to them. The poet compares such unshared wealth to a woman endowed with great beauty ('மிகநலம் பெற்றாள்') who lives in forced isolation ('தமியள்') and grows old ('மூத்து') without ever bringing joy to a partner or family. Just as her beauty goes to waste without fulfilling its natural purpose, the miser's wealth remains useless to society.

ai.literal: The wealth of he who is not desired is like a poisonous tree having ripened inside the middle of the village.
ai.translation: The wealth of a person who is not loved by anyone is like a poisonous tree bearing ripe fruit in the very middle of a village.
ai.modern: பிறரால் விரும்பப்படாதவனுடைய செல்வம், ஊரின் நடுவே நச்சு மரம் பழுத்து நிற்பதைப் போன்றது.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares the wealth of an unloved or miserly person to a poisonous tree bearing ripe fruit in the center of a village. Although the tree is full of fruit and highly visible to everyone, no one can eat it because it is toxic. Similarly, the wealth of a person who does not share or who is disliked by the community is useless to those around him. The key words 'நச்சப் படாதவன்' (he who is not desired or loved) and 'நச்சு மரம்' (poisonous tree) draw a sharp contrast between abundance and uselessness. The image of the tree in the 'நடுவூருள்' (middle of the village) emphasizes that the wealth is in plain sight but remains entirely out of reach for any beneficial purpose.

ai.literal: Love having forsaken, oneself having afflicted, virtue without considering, accumulated splendid wealth will be taken by others.
ai.translation: Others will possess the splendid wealth accumulated by one who has forsaken love, afflicted oneself with deprivation, and disregarded virtue.
ai.modern: அன்பைத் துறந்து, தன்னைத் தானே வருத்திக்கொண்டு, அறத்தையும் போற்றாமல் சேர்த்த சிறந்த செல்வத்தை மற்றவர்கள் எடுத்துக் கொள்வார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the futility of hoarding wealth through extreme greed. The poet explains that when a person accumulates 'splendid wealth' (ஒண்பொருள்) by abandoning love for fellow beings (அன்பொரீஇ), starving and afflicting their own body (தற்செற்று), and completely ignoring righteous deeds (அறநோக்காது), they do not get to enjoy it. Instead, that hard-earned wealth ultimately falls into the hands of strangers or others (பிறர் கொள்வார்). The verse teaches that wealth gathered without compassion, self-care, or virtue is entirely wasted on the hoarder.

ai.literal: The small refusal of wealthy people possessing excellence has the nature of being like the rain-cloud experiencing intense dryness.
ai.translation: The brief refusal of truly noble and wealthy people to give is like a rain-cloud temporarily running dry.
ai.modern: சிறப்புடைய செல்வர்களது தற்காலிகமான வெறுப்பு அல்லது கொடாமை, மழைமேகம் வறட்சி அடைந்ததைப் போன்ற தன்மையுடையது.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains the nature of generous people even when they temporarily stop giving. The 'small refusal' (ciṟutuni) of noble, wealthy individuals (cīruṭaic celvar) is not due to miserliness, but is a temporary phase. It is compared to a rain-cloud (māri) that has run dry (vaṟaṅkūrntu) for a brief period. Just as a dry cloud will eventually fill up and pour rain again, these noble souls will resume their benevolence once their temporary limitations pass.
